summary.text: At \(k=2\), using \(\binom n2=n(n-1)/2\) and \(\binom{n+2}2=(n+2)(n+1)/2\), every term of the binomial-denominator tail is exactly \(16\) times the corresponding product-denominator term. The latter tail converges and is strictly positive (already its \(n=3\) term is positive), so it cannot equal sixteen times itself, disproving the asserted equality of the two tails.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the universal statement by taking \(k=2\). For this value of \(k\), the first series in the conjecture is
\[
S:=\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}
 \frac{1}{n^3(n^2-1)^2(n^2-4)^2},
\]
and the second is
\[
T:=\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}
 \frac{1}{n\binom n2^2\binom{n+2}2^2(n-2)^2}.
\]
We will show that \(T=16S\), while \(S>0\). Consequently \(S\ne T\).

First simplify the summand of \(T\). For every integer \(n\ge 3\),
\[
\binom n2=\frac{n(n-1)}2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\binom{n+2}2=\frac{(n+2)(n+1)}2.
\]
It follows that the denominator in the \(n\)-th summand of \(T\) is
\[
\begin{aligned}
 n\binom n2^2\binom{n+2}2^2(n-2)^2
 &=n\left(\frac{n(n-1)}2\right)^2
      \left(\frac{(n+2)(n+1)}2\right)^2(n-2)^2\\
 &=\frac1{16}n^3(n-1)^2(n+1)^2(n-2)^2(n+2)^2\\
 &=\frac1{16}n^3(n^2-1)^2(n^2-4)^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
All these factors are nonzero when \(n\ge3\), so taking reciprocals gives
\[
\frac{1}{n\binom n2^2\binom{n+2}2^2(n-2)^2}
=
16\frac{1}{n^3(n^2-1)^2(n^2-4)^2}.
\]
Thus the second summand is exactly sixteen times the first summand for every index in the tail.

For completeness, these series converge. Indeed, for \(n\ge3\), both \((n^2-1)^2\) and \((n^2-4)^2\) are positive integers and in particular are at least \(1\). Hence
\[
0<\frac{1}{n^3(n^2-1)^2(n^2-4)^2}\le \frac1{n^3}.
\]
The \(p\)-series \(\sum_{n=3}^{\infty}n^{-3}\) converges, so comparison proves that \(S\) converges. The termwise identity above then also proves convergence of \(T\), and linearity of convergent series yields
\[
T=16S.
\]

Moreover, \(S\) is strictly positive. Every summand is nonnegative, and already the first one is
\[
\frac{1}{3^3(3^2-1)^2(3^2-4)^2}
=
\frac{1}{27\cdot64\cdot25}
=
\frac1{43200}>0.
\]
Therefore \(S\ge 1/43200>0\). In particular, \(16S>S\), and hence
\[
T=16S\ne S.
\]

The conjecture asserts, for every integer \(k\ge1\), that these two series are equal (and also that their common value equals a specified expression involving \(\zeta(3)\) and the OEIS numerator and denominator). The admissible value \(k=2\) already violates the first asserted equality. Therefore the entire universally quantified conjecture is false, irrespective of the additional claimed equality with \(\zeta(3)-a(k)/A281821(k)\).
